Priya. Before you disappear — what are you working on after this?
A second study, with the Amsterdam group. We are writing the protocol in November.
Sorry, I did not catch the month.
November. Would you like to be in it?
Yes. But let me be clear about what I can offer: our sample is small, sixty patients, and we do not have much data on the first three months.
That is not a problem. Your patients are the ones nobody else has.
Then I agree with the idea. I would rather start with one shared question than with a full protocol, though. It is faster.
I like that. Send me one question, in two lines, next week.
I will follow up on Monday. And thank you for the introduction to Amsterdam — that was the most useful thing that happened to me this week.
You did that yourself. I only pointed. Safe flight, Dejair.
What are you working on at the moment?
I work on neuropathic pain, and my main focus is leprosy.
Sorry, I did not catch that. Could you say it again?
I do not agree, and this is why.
I will follow up on Monday. Can we exchange contact details?

Dejair, it is Priya again. The congress finished an hour ago and I am at the airport, so forgive the noise. I wanted to say one thing before I forget it. When we met at the coffee break on the first day, you asked me what I was working on, and then you told me about leprosy in two sentences. Two sentences. That is why I remembered you three days later, and that is why I introduced you to the group from Amsterdam. Most people talk for five minutes and I remember nothing. So whatever you are doing with your English, keep doing that part. Send me the protocol when you can. And congratulations on the workshop. You spoke twice. I counted.

Before you go, three practical things from somebody who has done this eleven times. First, write the follow-up emails on the plane home, not next week. Next week never comes, and a contact that is not written down in seven days is gone. Second, do not send a long message. Two lines: where you met, and the one thing you promised. That is all anybody wants to read. Third, and this is the one people get wrong, write to the people who were kind to you, not only to the famous ones. The person who explained the room to you on the first morning is more likely to answer, and more likely to be useful, than the keynote speaker who shook two hundred hands.
